tiles.title: Variables and Core Data Types
tiles.summary: Learn to store values in variables using Python's assignment operator, understand naming rules, and recognise the four core scalar types: int, float, str and bool.

steps.title: Storing a value under a name
steps.lede: Before you can work with a delivery time in code, you need to give it a name you can refer back to.

blocks.text: Suppose you are processing a delivery order and need to keep track of how long it took. In Python, the equal sign (=) is used to assign a value to a variable, so writing delivery_minutes = 32 stores the number 32 under the name delivery_minutes. From that point on, any line that mentions delivery_minutes reads back the stored value.

A name only exists once something has been assigned to it. Referring to average_delivery_minutes before any earlier line has set it raises a NameError — Python does not invent a default value for you.

annotations.text: The name is rebound to 45; 32 is gone

blocks.change_summary: Assigning to delivery_minutes a second time replaces 32 with 45 — the name now refers to the new value.

steps.title: Naming rules and using stored values
steps.lede: Not every word is a valid variable name, and once a name holds a value you can use it in later expressions.

blocks.text: A valid variable name is made of letters, digits and underscores, cannot start with a digit, is case-significant (delivery_minutes and Delivery_Minutes are two different names), and cannot be a reserved keyword such as if, for or class.

Once a name holds a value, later code can use it in an expression. After orders_per_driver = 20 and days_worked = 5, a line such as orders_per_driver * days_worked reads back both stored values and computes a result from them.

steps.title: What happens when you use an unassigned name?
steps.lede: Test whether you can predict what Python does when a name has never been assigned.

steps.title: Assign and reassign delivery variables
steps.lede: Write Python to store delivery values, reassign one of them, and use the stored names in an expression.

steps.title: Four kinds of value: int, float, str and bool
steps.lede: Every value in Python has a type. Delivery data uses all four core scalar types.

blocks.text: Every value in Python has a type. In delivery data, an order id like 1042, a delivery time like 32.5, a city name like 'Lagos', and whether an order was late are four different kinds of value — Python has a core scalar type for each.

Whole numbers written without a decimal point — such as 2, 4 or 20 — have type int. A literal written with a fractional part, such as 5.0 or 1.6, has type float. So order_id = 1042 is an int, while delivery_minutes = 32.5 is a float.
Text values are of type str. They can be written with single quotes or double quotes with the same result — city = 'Lagos' and city = "Lagos" create the identical string value.
The bool type has exactly two values: True and False. For example, is_late = True records whether a delivery ran late, and there is no third bool value.

blocks.takeaway: 1042, 32.5, 'Lagos' and True are four different kinds of value — int, float, str and bool.

steps.title: Printing values and checking types
steps.lede: Two built-in tools let you see what a value is and what type it has.

blocks.text: print() writes the value of its argument. When that value is a string, print() writes it without the surrounding quotes — print(city) displays Lagos, not 'Lagos'.
The built-in type() function returns the type of its argument. print(type(delivery_minutes)) shows <class 'float'> and print(type(city)) shows <class 'str'>, so you can check a value's type directly.

steps.title: Predict print() output and check a type

steps.title: Create one variable of each core type

steps.title: What you learned
steps.lede: Key ideas from this tile.

blocks.text: = stores a value under a name; assigning again to that name replaces what it held; using a name that was never assigned raises a NameError. The four core scalar types are int, float, str and bool — type() tells you which one a value is.

blocks.title: Up next: Operators and Type Conversion
blocks.text: In the next tile you will use arithmetic and comparison operators on the values you have just learned to store.

remediation_steps.title: Why does Python raise NameError?
remediation_steps.lede: A name only exists after you assign it. Here is the contrast.

blocks.text: Python does not create a variable for you automatically. If you write print(average_delivery_minutes) before any line has assigned a value to that name, Python raises NameError: name 'average_delivery_minutes' is not defined. You must assign first: average_delivery_minutes = 32 before you can use it.

blocks.change_summary: Adding the assignment before the print removes the NameError.

remediation_steps.title: Assigning, reassigning and naming variables
remediation_steps.lede: A quick recap of the rules before you try the exercise again.

blocks.text: Use = to assign: delivery_minutes = 32. Assigning again to the same name replaces the old value — delivery_minutes = 45 makes the name hold 45. Once assigned, you can use the name in an expression: orders_per_driver * days_worked reads both stored values.

A valid name uses letters, digits and underscores, cannot start with a digit, is case-significant, and cannot be a reserved keyword such as if or for. delivery_minutes is valid; 1st_order and for are not.

remediation_steps.title: What print() and type() show
remediation_steps.lede: A clear contrast between what print() displays and what type() returns.

blocks.text: print() writes the value without quotes — print(city) displays Lagos, not 'Lagos'. type() returns the type object — print(type(city)) shows <class 'str'> and print(type(delivery_minutes)) shows <class 'float'>.

blocks.change_summary: Wrapping city in type() changes the output from the value to its type.

remediation_steps.title: The four core types and how to inspect them
remediation_steps.lede: A quick recap of int, float, str and bool, plus print() and type().

blocks.text: Whole numbers are int (order_id = 1042); numbers with a decimal point are float (delivery_minutes = 32.5); text in quotes is str (city = 'Lagos'); True or False is bool (is_late = True). These are the four core scalar types.
print(city) displays Lagos without quotes. print(type(city)) shows <class 'str'>. Use type() any time you need to confirm what kind of value a variable holds.

tiles.title: Comparison and Logical Operators
tiles.summary: Learn Python's arithmetic, comparison and logical operators, understand short-circuit evaluation and operator priority, and convert values between int, float and str.

steps.title: Seven operators for numeric work
steps.lede: Python gives you seven arithmetic operators — including two you may not have seen before.

blocks.text: Python provides seven arithmetic operators for numeric work. The familiar four — + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication) and / (division) — work as expected, but / always returns a float even when both operands are whole numbers: 8 / 2 gives 4.0, not 4. The ** operator raises a number to a power: 5 ** 2 is 25.

right.code:
(32 + 8) * 2    # parentheses group first
4 * 3.75 - 1    # int promoted to float

annotations.text: Result: 80 — parentheses force addition before multiplication

blocks.takeaway: 17 // 5 is 3 and 17 % 5 is 2; parentheses control evaluation order; mixing int and float promotes the result to float.

steps.title: Six operators that return True or False
steps.lede: Comparisons turn a question about data into a boolean value Python can branch on.

blocks.text: Comparing two values is how a question like 'is this delivery late?' becomes something Python can act on. The six comparison operators are < (less than), <= (less than or equal), > (greater than), >= (greater than or equal), == (equal) and != (not equal). Every comparison evaluates to exactly one of the two boolean values: True or False.

annotations.text: True for any city other than Lagos

blocks.takeaway: Each operator returns True or False; delivery_minutes > 60 is True for a 72-minute order and False for a 32-minute one.

steps.title: Choose the right comparison operator

steps.title: Combining conditions with and, or and not
steps.lede: Build compound conditions from simpler comparisons using Python's three logical operators.

blocks.text: A single comparison asks one question at a time. To combine conditions — 'is this delivery both late and far from the depot?' — Python provides three logical operators: or, and and not. In ascending priority order they are: or (lowest), and, not (highest among the three). When there are no parentheses, and binds more tightly than or.

x or y returns x if x is true, otherwise y. It is short-circuit: if is_late is True, Python never evaluates is_far. x and y returns x if x is false, otherwise y. It is also short-circuit: if is_late is False, Python skips is_far entirely.

left.code:
is_late or is_far
True or False
False or True
False or False

right.code:
is_late and is_far
True and True
True and False
False and True

annotations.text: True only if both conditions hold

blocks.takeaway: or is true when at least one operand is true; and is true only when both are; both short-circuit to skip the second operand when the result is already determined.

steps.title: not, priority and real-world compound conditions
steps.lede: not flips a boolean; priority rules determine how mixed expressions group without parentheses.

blocks.text: not x flips the boolean: not is_late is True when is_late is False, and False when is_late is True. not has lower priority than the comparison operators, so not delivery_minutes == 0 is read as not (delivery_minutes == 0), not as (not delivery_minutes) == 0.

A rule like 'flag this delivery if it is late or unusually far' reads directly as is_late or is_far. A stricter rule — 'flag it only if it is late and it is the driver's first week' — reads as is_late and is_first_week. and, or and not let you build one compound condition out of several simpler comparisons.

steps.title: Converting between strings and numbers
steps.lede: int(), float() and str() let you move values between types — but only when the format matches.

blocks.text: Data often arrives as the wrong type. A delivery time typed into a form as the text '32' cannot be used in arithmetic until it is converted to a number. Python provides three constructors for explicit conversion: int() and float() produce a number from a string or another numeric type, and str() turns any value into its string representation.

int('123') returns the integer 123. float('+1.23') returns the float 1.23. str(32) turns the integer 32 into the string '32'. These conversions work in both directions between numbers and their string representations.

Not every string can be converted. float() requires the string to match a numeric format — an optional sign, digits, and optionally a decimal point or exponent — after stripping surrounding whitespace. int() requires an integer string. A string that does not match raises a ValueError: int('3.5') fails because '3.5' is not an integer string.

annotations.text: String '32' — cannot add a number to it
TypeError: can only concatenate str to str

blocks.change_summary: Converting '32' from string to int with int() makes arithmetic possible; without conversion, adding a number raises a TypeError.

steps.title: What you learned
steps.lede: Key ideas from this tile.

blocks.text: Comparison operators (<, <=, >, >=, ==, !=) each return True or False. and, or and not combine those booleans into compound conditions; and has higher priority than or. Converting a string to a number only works when the string matches the format the target type accepts — otherwise the conversion raises a ValueError.

remediation_steps.title: Grouping with parentheses and mixed int/float
remediation_steps.lede: A clear contrast showing how parentheses change the result, and why mixing int and float gives a float.

blocks.text: Parentheses control evaluation order: (32 + 8) * 2 adds first, giving 80. Without parentheses, * runs before +. When you mix an int and a float in one operation, Python promotes the int to float: 4 * 3.75 - 1 gives 14.0, not 14.

blocks.change_summary: Adding parentheses changes the evaluation order and the result.

remediation_steps.title: Comparison operators and boolean results
remediation_steps.lede: A side-by-side contrast showing the same expression returning different booleans for different values.

blocks.text: The six comparison operators are < (less than), <= (less than or equal), > (greater than), >= (greater than or equal), == (equal) and != (not equal). Every comparison returns exactly True or False — never a number.

blocks.takeaway: The same expression delivery_minutes > 60 gives False for 32 and True for 72.

remediation_steps.title: Operator priority: and before or
remediation_steps.lede: A contrast showing how and and or group when there are no parentheses.

blocks.text: In ascending priority order the logical operators are: or (lowest), and, not. and binds more tightly than or, so is_late or is_far and is_first_week groups as is_late or (is_far and is_first_week). not has lower priority than comparison operators: not delivery_minutes == 0 means not (delivery_minutes == 0).

annotations.text: Groups as: is_late or (is_far and is_first_week)
Parentheses override priority — both sides must be true

blocks.change_summary: Without parentheses, and groups first; adding parentheses changes which conditions must both be true.

remediation_steps.title: Short-circuit evaluation in or and and
remediation_steps.lede: A side-by-side contrast showing when each operator stops evaluating early.

blocks.text: or short-circuits: if the first operand is True, Python returns it immediately without evaluating the second. and short-circuits: if the first operand is False, Python returns it immediately without evaluating the second. This means is_late or is_far only checks is_far when is_late is False, and is_late and is_far only checks is_far when is_late is True.

blocks.takeaway: Both operators skip the second operand when the first operand already determines the result.

remediation_steps.title: Converting between strings and numbers
remediation_steps.lede: A before/after showing what happens with and without int().

blocks.text: int('123') returns 123. float('+1.23') returns 1.23. str(32) returns '32'. These constructors convert between compatible types: a string of digits to int, a numeric-format string to float, any value to its string form.

blocks.change_summary: Wrapping '32' in int() converts it to the integer 32, making arithmetic possible.

remediation_steps.title: When type conversion raises ValueError
remediation_steps.lede: A contrast between a failing conversion and a working alternative.

blocks.text: float() requires the string to match a numeric format: an optional sign, digits, and optionally a decimal point or exponent, after stripping surrounding whitespace. int() requires an integer string — no decimal point. A string that does not match raises a ValueError: int('3.5') fails because '3.5' contains a decimal point.

annotations.text: ValueError — '3.5' is not an integer string
Result: 3.5 — decimal strings are valid for float()

blocks.takeaway: int() cannot parse a decimal string — it raises ValueError. float() accepts decimal strings; use float() when the string contains a decimal point.

tiles.title: Lists, Dictionaries, and Tuples
tiles.summary: Store ordered sequences in lists, map keys to values in dictionaries, and group fixed records in immutable tuples.

steps.title: Ordered, mutable sequences
steps.lede: A list stores an ordered sequence of values you can index, slice and modify.

blocks.text: Keeping five separate variables for five delivery times gets unwieldy fast. A list stores an ordered sequence of values in a single name: delivery_times = [32, 45, 21, 60, 18]. Items are indexed from 0 at the left and from -1 at the right, so delivery_times[0] is 32 and delivery_times[-1] is 18.

A slice extracts a sub-list: delivery_times[1:3] returns [45, 21]. The start index is included; the end index is excluded. delivery_times[-3:] returns the last three items. Lists are mutable: delivery_times[3] = 64 replaces the item at index 3 in place.

blocks.title: delivery_times — positive and negative indexes
blocks.alt_text: Array of five delivery times with positive indexes 0–4 above and negative indexes -5 to -1 below; a bracket marks slice [1:3] from index 1 (included) to index 3 (excluded), yielding [45, 21].

steps.title: Key-to-value lookup
steps.lede: A dictionary maps unique keys to values — look up a city by order ID, not by position.

blocks.text: Sometimes you need to look up a value by a meaningful key rather than by position. A dictionary is a collection of key: value pairs written inside braces, where keys must be unique: order_city = {1042: 'Lagos', 1043: 'Abuja', 1044: 'Kano'}. Retrieve a value by subscripting with its key: order_city[1042] returns 'Lagos'.

Store or update a value by assigning to a key: order_city[1044] = 'Kano' adds a new entry; assigning to an existing key replaces its value. The get() method returns None (or a specified default) instead of raising an error when a key is absent: order_city.get(9999) returns None rather than crashing.
Subscripting a key that is not in the dictionary raises a KeyError: order_city[9999] fails if no order 9999 was ever added. Use get() when you are not certain the key exists.

blocks.alt_text: Mapping diagram: keys 1042, 1043, 1044 each point to their city values; key 9999 points to a KeyError node showing what happens when a missing key is subscripted.

steps.title: Immutable sequences and unpacking
steps.lede: A tuple groups a fixed set of values; unpacking hands each piece back to its own name.

blocks.text: A tuple groups a small, fixed set of values together. It is written as comma-separated values, with or without surrounding parentheses: order = 1042, 'Lagos', 32 or order = (1042, 'Lagos', 32). Python shows tuples enclosed in parentheses on output.

Tuples are immutable: once created, an item cannot be reassigned. order[0] = 1099 raises a TypeError. Also, enclosing a single value in parentheses does not make it a tuple — singleton = ('Lagos') is still just the string 'Lagos'. A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma: singleton = 'Lagos', ⟦C.f3⟧

annotations.text: Three values packed into one tuple

blocks.change_summary: Unpacking hands each element of the tuple back to its own name — order_id, city and minutes are now separate variables. ⟦C.f3⟧

steps.title: What you learned
steps.lede: Key ideas from this tile.

blocks.text: A list is an ordered, mutable sequence indexed from 0; slices use start-included, end-excluded bounds; index assignment replaces an item in place and append() adds one at the end. A dictionary maps unique keys to values; subscripting a missing key raises a KeyError — use get() to avoid it. A tuple groups a fixed set of values that cannot be reassigned; unpacking distributes each element to its own name.

tiles.title: Sets and Strings
tiles.summary: Use sets to collect unique values and test membership, combine sets with union and intersection, and build readable messages with f-strings and format specifiers.

steps.title: Unique, unordered collections
steps.lede: A set stores only distinct values — duplicates are automatically removed.

blocks.text: Sometimes you only care about which distinct values appear — which cities orders were delivered to, with no duplicates. A set is an unordered collection with no duplicate elements, used for membership testing and eliminating duplicate entries.

Curly braces or the set() function create a set. set() must be used for an empty set, because {} creates an empty dictionary instead. set() can also build a set from another collection: cities = set(['Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Lagos', 'Kano']) produces {'Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano'} — the duplicate 'Lagos' is collapsed to one entry.

blocks.change_summary: Passing the list through set() collapses the repeated 'Lagos' to a single entry, leaving only unique cities.

blocks.text: Test whether a value is in the set with the `in` operator: `'Lagos' in cities` returns `True` if `'Lagos'` is in the set, and `False` otherwise. This membership test is the primary reason to use a set rather than a list when you only need to check presence. ⟦A.f4 A:tb4⟧

steps.title: Union and intersection
steps.lede: | combines two sets; & finds what they share.

blocks.text: Set objects support mathematical operations. Union (a | b) gives all elements from both sets. Intersection (a & b) gives only elements present in both: week1_cities & week2_cities gives cities that appeared in both weeks.

steps.title: Embedding values and formatting numbers
steps.lede: f-strings embed variable values directly in a string; a format specifier controls how numbers are displayed.

blocks.text: A quote character can be embedded in a string without escaping it by using the other kind of quote. Writing "This delivery wasn't late" inside double quotes needs no escaping; the same text inside single quotes would need the apostrophe escaped as \'.

An f-string is a string literal prefixed with f or F that embeds the value of a Python expression inside the string by writing the expression in curly brackets: f"Delivery to {city} took {delivery_minutes} minutes" substitutes in the current values of city and delivery_minutes.

An optional format specifier follows the expression after a colon, controlling how the value is displayed. f"Average: {avg_minutes:.2f} minutes" produces 'Average: 32.67 minutes' when avg_minutes is 32.666 — the .2f specifier rounds to two decimal places.

blocks.change_summary: Adding :.2f after the expression rounds the output to two decimal places — the {value:.2f} part and its rounded result.

remediation_steps.title: Union and intersection on sets
remediation_steps.lede: A side-by-side contrast showing | and & on the same two sets.

blocks.text: | (union) gives all elements from either set — no duplicates. & (intersection) gives only the elements present in both sets. If week1_cities = {'Lagos', 'Abuja'} and week2_cities = {'Abuja', 'Kano'}, then week1_cities | week2_cities is {'Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano'} and week1_cities & week2_cities is {'Abuja'}.

blocks.takeaway: | combines both sets; & keeps only what they have in common.

blocks.text: A quote character can be embedded in a string without escaping it by enclosing the string in the other kind of quote. "This delivery wasn't late" uses double quotes, so the apostrophe in wasn't needs no backslash. Inside single quotes the same apostrophe would need escaping: 'This delivery wasn\'t late'.

blocks.text: Branching on data: if, elif, else

Not every line of code should always run — sometimes what happens next depends on the data. An if statement executes its block only when its condition is true. You can add zero or more elif parts after an if, and an optional else at the end; elif is short for 'else if' and keeps the code flat instead of deeply nested.

blocks.text: Visiting every item: the for loop

Once delivery times are collected in a list, you'll want to do something with every single one of them, not just one at a time by hand. Python's for statement iterates over the items of any sequence — such as a list or a string — in the order they appear. Each pass binds the loop variable to the next item:

for minutes in delivery_times:
    print(minutes)

This prints every delivery time in delivery_times, one per pass.

steps.lede: One branch, every item.

blocks.text: Reading top to bottom, exactly one branch of an if/elif/else chain runs for any given delivery time — the first whose condition is true, or else if none are. A for loop visits every item of a sequence such as a list once, in the order the items appear, which is what you need to process each delivery time in turn.

blocks.text: Next you'll learn how to keep a loop running as long as a condition holds — and how to exit or skip iterations mid-loop.

remediation_steps.title: When does an if block run?
remediation_steps.lede: Let's revisit the rule for when an if block executes.

blocks.text: Reminder: when does an if block run?

An if statement executes its block only when its condition is true — not every time the code runs. If delivery_minutes = 30 and the condition is delivery_minutes > 45, the block is skipped entirely. The block runs only when the condition evaluates to True.

remediation_steps.title: Which branch runs in a chain?
remediation_steps.lede: Let's revisit how an if/elif/else chain selects exactly one branch.

blocks.text: Reminder: which branch runs in a chain?

An if/elif/else chain evaluates conditions one by one from top to bottom. The first condition that is true wins — its block runs and all others are skipped. If no condition is true, the else block (if present) runs. With delivery_minutes = 30: the first condition (< 15) is false, the second (< 45) is true, so category = 'normal' runs and the else branch is skipped.

remediation_steps.title: What value does the loop variable hold?
remediation_steps.lede: Let's revisit how the loop variable takes each value in turn.

blocks.text: Reminder: what value does the loop variable hold?

Each pass through a for loop binds the loop variable to the next item of the sequence. With delivery_times = [32, 45, 21, 60, 18], the first pass sets minutes = 32, the second sets minutes = 45, and so on. The variable takes each value in order, one per pass.

steps.title: Repeating while a condition holds: the while loop
steps.lede: Keep processing deliveries as long as there are still orders to handle.

blocks.text: Repeating while a condition holds: the while loop

Sometimes you don't know in advance how many times you'll need to repeat something — you just want to keep going as long as some condition holds. A while loop executes its body repeatedly as long as its condition remains true; the condition can be a comparison, such as a < 10.

The body is indented beneath the while line, and something in the body must change what the condition checks — otherwise the loop never stops:

pending = 3
while pending > 0:
    print('deliveries left:', pending)
    pending = pending - 1

Each pass prints the current count and decreases pending by 1, so the loop stops once pending reaches 0.

blocks.text: Steering mid-loop: break and continue

The break statement exits the innermost enclosing for or while loop immediately — useful for stopping a search over delivery orders as soon as the one you want is found. The continue statement skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one — for example, skipping a delivery record that's missing a time without exiting the whole loop.

Use break to exit a loop early and continue to skip the rest of the current iteration.

remediation_steps.title: The body must change what the condition checks
remediation_steps.lede: Let's revisit why the loop body must update the condition variable.

blocks.text: Reminder: the body must change what the condition checks

The body of a while loop must change what the condition checks — otherwise the condition stays true forever and the loop never stops. In the pending example, pending = pending - 1 decreases pending each pass, so pending > 0 eventually becomes false and the loop exits.

remediation_steps.title: continue vs break
remediation_steps.lede: Let's revisit the difference between continue and break.

blocks.text: Reminder: continue vs break

continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one — the loop keeps running. break exits the innermost loop entirely — no more iterations happen. Use continue to skip a bad record; use break to stop searching once you've found what you need.

steps.title: Building lists and dicts in one line: comprehensions
steps.lede: Replace multi-line loops with compact, readable expressions.

blocks.text: Building lists and dicts in one line: comprehensions

Building a new list from an existing one by looping is common enough that Python has a shorthand for it. A list comprehension consists of brackets containing an expression followed by a for clause, and optionally one or more for or if clauses; it produces a new list by evaluating the expression for each item — [minutes * 2 for minutes in delivery_times] doubles every value.

Add an if clause to filter the source: [minutes for minutes in delivery_times if minutes >= 45] keeps only the delivery times that satisfy that condition. Dict comprehensions work the same way with curly braces and a key: value expression — {city: len(city) for city in ('Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano')} maps each city name to its length.

# Equivalent list comprehension
doubled = [minutes * 2 for minutes in delivery_times if minutes >= 45]

steps.title: Looping over any collection: lists, dicts, sets and tuples
steps.lede: The same for loop syntax works on every collection — what changes is what you get back.

blocks.text: Looping over any collection: lists, dicts, sets and tuples

You've already looped over lists with for. The same for x in ... pattern works on other collections, but what you get back per pass differs. Looping directly over a dictionary yields its keys — for order_id in order_city: visits each order id, not each city. To get both key and value together, use .items(): for order_id, city in order_city.items(): print(order_id, city).

A set's elements may come out in a different order than expected when iterated over, because a set is unordered — looping over a set of cities won't necessarily visit them in the order they were added. Tuples are a sequence type, so a for loop visits their items in order the same way it does for a list — for value in order: visits 1042, then 'Lagos', then 32, when order = (1042, 'Lagos', 32).

blocks.text: Reminder: dict comprehension syntax

Dict comprehensions use curly braces with a key: value expression before the for clause — {city: len(city) for city in ('Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano')} maps each city name to its length. The key and value expressions can be any valid Python expression; the result is a new dictionary, not a list.

remediation_steps.title: Sets are unordered

blocks.text: Reminder: sets are unordered

A set's elements may come out in a different order than expected when iterated over, because a set is unordered. Looping over {'Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano'} won't necessarily visit them in the order they were written — the order can vary between runs. If order matters, use a list or tuple instead.

tiles.title: Defining Functions, Parameters, and Return Values

steps.title: Define once, run whenever you need it
steps.lede: A function packages a block of code under a name so you can run it as many times as you like without copying it.

blocks.text: The keyword `def` introduces a function definition: `def summarize_delivery():` gives the function its name and an empty parameter list. The statements that form the body start on the next line and must be indented. Writing the `def` block only stores the function under that name — nothing in the body runs yet.

Calling the function by its name followed by parentheses — `summarize_delivery()` — is what actually runs the body. You can call the same function multiple times; each call runs the body from the top.

steps.title: Give your function the inputs it needs
steps.lede: Parameters let a function work with different values on each call instead of always doing the same thing.

blocks.text: The formal parameters of a function are named in its `def` statement's parenthesised list. `def classify_delivery(minutes):` declares one parameter, `minutes`. Inside the body, `minutes` refers to whatever value was passed when the function was called.

When you call a function with positional arguments, the first argument fills the first parameter slot, the second fills the second, and so on. For `def delivery_summary(city, minutes):`, calling `delivery_summary('Lagos', 32)` sets `city` to `'Lagos'` and `minutes` to `32`.

steps.title: Hand a result back to the caller
steps.lede: A function that only prints its result can't be reused — the caller needs a `return` statement to get the value back.

blocks.text: A `return` statement sends a value back to the code that called the function. `return category` gives the caller access to the string `category` computed inside the function. Without `return`, the caller receives `None` — the built-in empty value Python uses when nothing is explicitly returned.

The returned value can be stored in a variable for later use. After `result = classify_delivery(32)`, the variable `result` holds whatever `classify_delivery` returned, so later code can reuse `result` without calling the function again.

steps.title: Optional parameters and named arguments
steps.lede: Default values let callers omit arguments; keyword arguments let callers name them explicitly.

blocks.text: Specifying a default value for a parameter — `def ask_ok(prompt, retries=4):` — creates a function that can be called with fewer arguments than it is defined to accept. Calling `ask_ok('Delete this order?')` works and uses `4` for `retries`.

A function can also be called using keyword arguments of the form `kwarg=value` — `ask_ok(prompt='Delete this order?', retries=2)`. In a call, keyword arguments must follow any positional arguments. All keyword arguments must match one of the function's parameters, and no parameter may receive a value more than once.

A default value is evaluated only once, at the point the function is defined — not on each call. If that default is a mutable object such as a list, the same object is shared across calls and can accumulate changes unless the function creates a fresh value each time.

steps.title: Where Python looks for a name
steps.lede: A name created inside a function lives in that function's local table — it doesn't automatically reach the outside world.

blocks.text: All variable assignments in a function store the value in that function's local symbol table. A name like `total` assigned inside a function is a different variable from any `total` that exists outside it.

For a function that is not nested inside another, variable references inside it first look in the local symbol table, then the global symbol table, and finally the table of built-in names. So a name assigned only outside the function is still readable inside it — Python finds it in the global table once the local lookup fails.

A global variable cannot be directly assigned a value from inside a function unless it is named in a `global` statement. Without `global total`, writing `total = 0` inside a function creates a new local `total` and leaves the global `total` unchanged. The global may still be read without the statement.

steps.title: Functions: what you've learned
steps.lede: Five ideas that make functions reusable and predictable.

blocks.text: `def` creates a reusable block of code under a name; calling that name followed by parentheses is what actually runs it. Parameters name the inputs a function expects; arguments in a specific call supply the actual values. `return` turns a function from something that does an action into something that hands back a result the caller can store and reuse. A function with no `return` statement (or a bare `return`) hands back `None` to its caller. Assigning to a name inside a function makes it local by default; only reading reaches out to a global unless a `global` statement says otherwise.

remediation_steps.title: What makes a function definition?
remediation_steps.lede: A function definition always starts with the keyword def.

blocks.text: The keyword `def` introduces a function definition, followed by the function's name and a parenthesised list of parameters. `def summarize_delivery():` is a definition — it stores the function but does not run it. A bare call like `summarize_delivery()` without a preceding `def` would raise a `NameError`.

remediation_steps.title: Positional arguments fill slots in order
remediation_steps.lede: The first argument always goes to the first parameter, the second to the second.

blocks.text: When you call `delivery_summary('Lagos', 32)`, Python places `'Lagos'` in the first parameter slot (`city`) and `32` in the second (`minutes`) — strictly by position. Swapping the arguments to `delivery_summary(32, 'Lagos')` would swap their meanings, giving `city` the value `32`.

remediation_steps.title: return sends a value back; print does not
remediation_steps.lede: Only return gives the caller a value to store.

blocks.text: A `return` statement sends a value back to the code that called the function — `result = classify_delivery(32)` stores whatever `classify_delivery` returns. A function that only calls `print()` hands back `None` to its caller, not the printed text. To store and reuse a result, the function must use `return`.

remediation_steps.title: Mutable defaults are shared across calls
remediation_steps.lede: A default value is created once — not freshly on each call.

blocks.text: A default value is evaluated only once, at the point the function is defined — not on each call. If that default is a mutable object such as a list, the same object is shared across all calls and can accumulate changes. To avoid this, create a fresh value inside the function body rather than in the parameter default.

remediation_steps.title: Local first, then global
remediation_steps.lede: Python checks the local table before the global one.

blocks.text: All variable assignments in a function store the value in that function's local symbol table. When Python looks up a name inside a function, it checks the local table first, then the global table, then built-ins. A name assigned only outside the function is still readable inside — Python finds it in the global table once the local lookup fails.

remediation_steps.title: Assigning to a global requires the global statement
remediation_steps.lede: Reading a global is free; writing to it requires declaring it.

blocks.text: A global variable cannot be directly assigned a value from inside a function unless it is named in a `global` statement. Without `global total`, writing `total = 0` inside a function creates a new local `total` and leaves the global `total` unchanged. The global may still be read without the statement.

steps.title: Catch failures before they crash your script
steps.lede: A try/except block lets your code attempt something that might fail and respond to the specific failure instead of stopping entirely.

blocks.text: The `try` statement first executes the statements in its `try` clause. If no exception occurs, the `except` clause is skipped and execution continues normally after the block.

If an exception occurs during the `try` clause and its type matches the exception named after `except`, the `except` clause is executed and execution continues after the `try`/`except` block. An unmatched exception propagates upward.

Wrapping `int(input(...))` in a `try` clause with `except ValueError` lets the program print `'Oops! That was no valid number. Try again...'` instead of crashing when the conversion fails. If the input is `'twelve'`, `int()` raises a `ValueError`, the `except` clause runs, and the program continues.

blocks.alt_text: Flowchart: 'Execute try clause' leads to a decision 'Exception occurred?'. No path goes to 'Skip except clause' then 'Continue'. Yes path goes to 'Exception raised', then 'Type matches except?'. Yes path goes to 'Run except clause' then 'Continue'.

steps.title: Bring in code from other files
steps.lede: A module is a file of Python definitions; import gives your script access to them.

blocks.text: A module is a file containing Python definitions and statements. Definitions from a module can be imported into another module or into the main script with the `import` statement — `import fibo` makes the module available under the name `fibo`.

Importing a module this way does not add the names defined in it directly to the current namespace — it adds the module name. Its functions are accessed through that name: `fibo.fib(1000)`. The `from module import name` variant imports names directly into the current namespace, so `from fibo import fib` lets you call `fib(500)` without the module prefix.

Python comes with a library of standard modules imported the same way. `import sys` makes the `sys` module's names — such as `sys.path` — available through `sys`. `import math` gives access to `math.sqrt`, `math.pi`, and so on.

import fibo

fibo.fib(1000)   # module prefix required
fibo.fib2(100)

annotations.text: Names accessed through the module name

right.code:

fib(500)         # no prefix needed

blocks.takeaway: import module keeps names behind the module prefix; from module import name brings them directly into scope.

blocks.text: `try`/`except` lets the program attempt something that might fail and respond to the specific failure rather than stopping entirely. If no exception occurs, the `except` clause is skipped; if the exception type matches, the `except` clause runs and execution continues. `import` gives you access to code written in another file — either through the module's name (`import fibo`, `fibo.fib(...)`) or directly by name (`from fibo import fib`, `fib(...)`).

remediation_steps.title: Catching a ValueError from int()
remediation_steps.lede: The except clause only runs when the exception type matches.

blocks.text: Wrapping `int(input(...))` in a `try` clause with `except ValueError` catches the error when the input cannot be converted. If the typed text is `'twelve'`, `int()` raises a `ValueError`, the `except` clause runs and prints a message, and the program continues. If the input is `'12'`, `int()` succeeds, the `except` clause is skipped, and `minutes_late` holds `12`.

remediation_steps.title: import vs from … import
remediation_steps.lede: The two forms differ in what lands in your namespace.

blocks.text: `import fibo` adds the module name `fibo` to your namespace; you then call `fibo.fib(1000)`. `from fibo import fib` adds the name `fib` directly, so you call `fib(500)` without a prefix. Both forms import from the same module file — they differ only in what name lands in your namespace.

steps.title: Open a file and read its contents
steps.lede: Delivery records often live in files on disk. open() and with give you a safe, automatic way to read them.

blocks.text: `open(filename, mode)` returns a file object. The mode can be `'r'` to read, `'w'` to write (erasing an existing file of the same name), or `'a'` to append; `'r'` is assumed if mode is omitted. `open('orders.txt')` opens `orders.txt` for reading.

It is good practice to use the `with` keyword when working with a file object, because it closes the file automatically after its block finishes — even if an exception is raised. `with open('orders.txt') as f:` opens the file and assigns the file object to `f`; the file is closed when the `with` block exits.

`f.read()` reads the file's entire contents and returns them as a string in text mode. Once the end of the file is reached, further calls to `f.read()` return an empty string. `csv.DictReader(f)` creates a reader that maps each row of a CSV file to a dict, using the first row's values as keys by default.

before.code:
# Raw text read — one big string
with open('orders.txt') as f:
    contents = f.read()
print(contents)

after.code:
import csv

# CSV read — each row is a dict
with open('orders.csv', newline='') as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    for row in reader:
        print(row['order_id'], row['city'])

annotations.text: Each row is a dict keyed by the header names

blocks.change_summary: Switch from f.read() (one string) to csv.DictReader (one dict per row, keyed by column name).

steps.title: Write text and CSV rows to a file
steps.lede: f.write() sends a string to a file; csv.DictWriter maps dicts to rows.

blocks.text: `f.write(string)` writes the contents of `string` to the file, returning the number of characters written. Opening with mode `'w'` erases any existing file of the same name before writing; mode `'a'` appends to the end.

`csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=['order_id', 'city'])` creates a writer that maps a dict to a row. `writer.writeheader()` writes the header row and `writer.writerow(dict)` writes one data row, in the order given by `fieldnames`.

A CSV file used with the `csv` module should be opened with `newline=''` — for example, `open('orders.csv', 'w', newline='')`. This prevents the csv module from seeing extra blank lines on some platforms.

A complete read-then-write workflow: open `orders.csv` with `newline=''` and `csv.DictReader` to iterate rows, then open `lagos_orders.csv` for writing with `csv.DictWriter`, call `writeheader()`, and call `writerow(row)` for each Lagos order. Both `open()` calls use `with` so files close automatically.

steps.title: Read and write CSV rows as dicts
steps.lede: Use csv.DictReader to read orders.csv and csv.DictWriter to write a filtered output file.

steps.title: File I/O: what you've learned
steps.lede: Four ideas that connect your script to data on disk.

blocks.text: Reading and writing files is how a program's delivery data gets in from, and results get out to, storage that outlives the program run. `open()` and `with` manage the connection and guarantee the file closes. The `csv` module adds structured row-by-row access: `csv.DictReader` maps each row to a dict keyed by the header names, and `csv.DictWriter` maps dicts back to rows.

blocks.title: Up next: PEP 8 style

remediation_steps.title: open() modes and f.read() / f.write()
remediation_steps.lede: The mode string controls whether you read, write, or append.

blocks.text: `open(filename, mode)` returns a file object. Mode `'r'` reads (default), `'w'` writes and erases any existing file of the same name, `'a'` appends. `f.read()` returns the file's contents as a string; once the end is reached, further calls return an empty string. `f.write(string)` writes the string and returns the number of characters written.

remediation_steps.title: The with statement closes the file automatically
remediation_steps.lede: with guarantees cleanup even when an exception occurs.

blocks.text: It is good practice to use the `with` keyword when working with a file object, because it closes the file automatically after its block finishes — even if an exception is raised. `with open('orders.txt') as f:` opens the file and assigns the file object to `f`; the file is closed when the `with` block exits, without needing an explicit `f.close()` call.

steps.title: Write code others can read
steps.lede: PEP 8 is Python's style guide. Its recommendations make code easier to read for the next person — including a later you.

blocks.text: PEP 8 recommends using 4 spaces per indentation level, with spaces rather than tabs as the preferred indentation method, and limiting all lines to a maximum of 79 characters. PEP 8 also recommends avoiding extraneous whitespace — such as immediately inside parentheses, brackets or braces, or immediately before a comma, semicolon, or colon.

PEP 8 recommends that function and variable names be lowercase, with words separated by underscores as necessary for readability — `delivery_minutes` rather than `deliveryMinutes` or `DeliveryMinutes`.

steps.title: PEP 8: what you've learned
steps.lede: Four recommendations that make Python code readable.

blocks.text: PEP 8 recommends 4 spaces per indentation level (not tabs), lines of at most 79 characters, no extraneous whitespace inside parentheses or before commas, and `lowercase_with_underscores` names for functions and variables. These are recommendations for readability — following them makes code easier to read for the next person, including a later you.

remediation_steps.title: Extraneous whitespace: what to avoid
remediation_steps.lede: PEP 8 names specific places where extra spaces hurt readability.

blocks.text: PEP 8 recommends avoiding extraneous whitespace immediately inside parentheses, brackets or braces — `spam(ham[1], {eggs: 2})` rather than `spam( ham[ 1], { eggs: 2} )`. It also recommends no space immediately before a comma, semicolon, or colon — `x, y = 1, 2` rather than `x , y = 1 , 2`.
